reason: B opens with the Zong killings as a sustained, concrete narrative and lets the legal and economic argument grow out of that scene, so a general reader is pulled forward by people and stakes rather than by exposition. A instead cycles through descriptive set-pieces (plantation routine, codes, ships, revolution, abolition) that restate the same thesis - law made violence property - in successive paragraphs, and it repeats the same statutes (1662 Virginia, 1740 South Carolina, the Code Noir, Barbados 1661, the Dolben Act) in more than one section. B moves: Zong to courtroom to Barbados code to Jamaican credit to Brazil and Saint-Domingue to Toussaint to Haiti to Louisiana, each step causally hooked to the last, and it ends on a real argumentative question rather than A's stray dangling sentence about the Code Noir.
